chmmc-2013-mixer-01.title: A takes everything
chmmc-2013-mixer-01.body:
Because $k$ may be any number from $1$ to $n$ inclusive, $A$ can take all $n$ marbles on the first turn and take the last marble immediately. So $A$ wins for every $n>1$, there is no $n$ for which $B$ wins, and the (empty) sum is $0$.

**Answer: 0**

chmmc-2013-mixer-02.title: Place vowels and consonants
chmmc-2013-mixer-02.body:
The letters are $4$ vowels (A, e, a, o) and $5$ consonants (l, j, n, d, r); A and a are the same letter, so the vowels can be ordered in $\frac{4!}{2}=12$ ways and the consonants in $5!=120$ ways. Exactly one adjacent vowel pair means the vowels form three groups in a row (one group of two, two single vowels): $3$ choices for which group is the double. Consecutive groups need at least one consonant between them, so put one consonant in each of the two interior gaps and distribute the remaining $3$ consonants among the $4$ gaps (before, two between, after): $\binom{6}{3}=20$ ways. So there are $3\cdot20=60$ patterns and the total is $60\cdot120\cdot12=86400$.

**Answer: 86400**

chmmc-2013-mixer-02.title: Brute force
chmmc-2013-mixer-02.body:
Listing all distinct arrangements of the nine letters by computer (there are $9!/2=181440$) and counting those with exactly one adjacent pair of vowels gives $86400$.

**Answer: 86400**

chmmc-2013-mixer-04.title: Unfold the box
chmmc-2013-mixer-04.body:
Reflect the box instead of the beam: the beam becomes the straight line through the corner in direction $(1,1,1)$, i.e. the points $(t,t,t)$. It reaches a corner of some reflected copy when $t$ is a multiple of each of $48$, $140$ and $126$, first at $t=\operatorname{lcm}(48,140,126)=5040$. The distance travelled is $\sqrt{t^2+t^2+t^2}=5040\sqrt3$.

(The official key lists $5040$, the common coordinate; the actual path length is $5040\sqrt3$.)

**Answer: $5040\sqrt3$**

chmmc-2013-mixer-05.title: Catalan number
chmmc-2013-mixer-05.body:
Dividing a convex $n$-gon into $n-2$ triangles by diagonals is a triangulation; the number of triangulations of an $n$-gon is the Catalan number $C_{n-2}$. For $n=7$ this is $C_5=\frac1{6}\binom{10}{5}=42$.

**Answer: 42**

chmmc-2013-mixer-05.title: Recursion
chmmc-2013-mixer-05.body:
Let $T_n$ be the number of triangulations of an $n$-gon, $T_2=1$. Fixing the triangle on one side gives $T_n=\sum_{k=2}^{n-1}T_kT_{n-k+1}$, so $T_3=1$, $T_4=2$, $T_5=5$, $T_6=14$, $T_7=42$.

**Answer: 42**

chmmc-2013-mixer-06.title: Factor and count
chmmc-2013-mixer-06.body:
$x^3+7x^2-14x-48=(x+2)(x+8)(x-3)$, so the greatest root is $a=3$. Then $b=\binom{9}{3}=84$ and $\frac b2=42$.

**Answer: 42**

chmmc-2013-mixer-07.title: Egyptian fractions
chmmc-2013-mixer-07.body:
The equation says $\frac1a+\frac1b+\frac1c+\frac1d=1$. The equation says $\frac1a+\frac1b+\frac1c+\frac1d=1$. To make $d$ as large as possible, $\frac1a+\frac1b+\frac1c$ must be as close to $1$ as possible from below. For three unit fractions the largest sum below $1$ is $\frac12+\frac13+\frac17=\frac{41}{42}$ (if $a\ge3$ the sum is at most $1$ with only small values of $d$; with $a=2$, $b=3$ the third fraction must be less than $\frac16$, and $c=7$ is the closest; with $b\ge4$ the sum is at most $\frac12+\frac14+\frac14=1$, which only gives small $d$). Then $\frac1d=1-\frac{41}{42}=\frac1{42}$, so $d=42$.

**Answer: 42**

chmmc-2013-mixer-08.title: Slack variable
chmmc-2013-mixer-08.body:
Add a slack variable $x_{13}\ge0$ so that $x_1+\cdots+x_{13}=17$. By stars and bars the number of solutions is $\binom{17+12}{12}=\binom{29}{12}=51\,895\,935$. With $2b\le a$ the representation is $a=29$, $b=12$ (the other form $\binom{29}{17}$ has $2b>a$), so $a+b=41$.

**Answer: 41**

chmmc-2013-mixer-08.title: Hockey stick
chmmc-2013-mixer-08.body:
Summing over the total $s=0,\dots,17$ the number of solutions $\binom{s+11}{11}$ gives $\sum_{s=0}^{17}\binom{s+11}{11}=\binom{29}{12}$ by the hockey stick identity, again $a+b=41$.

**Answer: 41**

chmmc-2013-mixer-09.title: Power of a point, then Heron
chmmc-2013-mixer-09.body:
By the tangent-secant theorem, $AB^2=BD\cdot BC$, so $BC=\dfrac{(27/2)^2}{243/34}=\dfrac{51}{2}$. The triangle has sides $15,\ \frac{27}{2},\ \frac{51}{2}$ with semi-perimeter $s=27$, and Heron's formula gives $$\sqrt{27\cdot12\cdot\tfrac{27}{2}\cdot\tfrac32}=\sqrt{6561}=81.$$

**Answer: 81**

chmmc-2013-mixer-10.title: All bracketed terms are equal
chmmc-2013-mixer-10.body:
$2^{\log x}=10^{\log2\cdot\log x}=x^{\log 2}$, so every bracket equals the same number $T$ and the expression is $T^{T^{T^{\cdots}}}=2$. The tower satisfies $T^{\,\text{tower}}=\text{tower}$, i.e. $T^2=2$, so $T=\sqrt2$. Then $2^{\log x}=2^{1/2}$ gives $\log x=\frac12$, $x=\sqrt{10}$, $n=10$ and $n^2=100$.

**Answer: 100**

chmmc-2013-mixer-13.title: Try small squares
chmmc-2013-mixer-13.body:
Here $3xz=105$ and $f(n)=(\text{number of distinct digits of } n)^2$ (any ordered pair of the available digits, as the example $f(15)=4$ shows). So $w\in\{1,4,9\}$ for a number with up to three digits: $w=1$ gives $f(104)=9$; $w=4$ gives $f(101)=4$ (digits $0,1$); $w=9$ gives $f(96)=4\neq9$. Hence $w=4$.

(This problem was the first of a chain: $w=4$ here, $x=5$ in problem 14, $z=7$ in problem 16.)

**Answer: 4**

chmmc-2013-mixer-14.title: Central binomial coefficient
chmmc-2013-mixer-14.body:
The coefficient is $\binom{2x}{x}$ and $5z^2+2w-1=245+8-1=252$. The central binomial coefficients are $2,6,20,70,252,\dots$ for $x=1,2,3,4,5$, so $x=5$.

**Answer: 5**

chmmc-2013-mixer-15.title: Orthocenters
chmmc-2013-mixer-15.body:
With $AE=15$, $ED=13$, $AD=14$. Since $AD$ is a diameter, $\angle ABD=\angle ACD=90^\circ$, so $DB\perp AE$ and $AC\perp DE$: $F$ is the orthocenter of $\triangle AED$, and $EG$ is its altitude to $AD$. By Heron, $s=21$ and the area is $\sqrt{21\cdot6\cdot8\cdot7}=84$, so $EG=\frac{2\cdot84}{14}=12$. Also $AG=\frac{15^2+14^2-13^2}{2\cdot14}=9$ and $GD=5$.

For an orthocenter $F$ with foot $G$ on $AD$, $GF\cdot GE=GA\cdot GD$ (the triangles $AGF$ and $EGD$ are similar). So $FG=\frac{9\cdot5}{12}=\frac{15}4$.

(The official solution only computes $EG=12$.)

**Answer: $\dfrac{15}{4}$**

chmmc-2013-mixer-16.title: Squares
chmmc-2013-mixer-16.body:
$n^2+n^3=n^2(n+1)$ is a perfect square iff $n+1$ is. For $n\in\{4,\dots,80\}$, $n+1$ ranges over $5,\dots,81$, which contains the squares $9,16,25,36,49,64,81$. So $z=7$.

**Answer: 7**
